Heterogeneous operator fusion in ML compiler backends asks: given a computation graph whose nodes span multiple hardware domains (e.g., CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, memory subsystems, potentially CPU fallbacks), where do you cut the graph into fused kernels versus separate dispatch calls, and how does that decision change when tensor shapes aren't known until runtime? The key concepts are fusion boundaries (the cuts), operator heterogeneity (nodes differ in hardware target, memory layout requirements, or numerics), kernel code generation (what the compiler emits per fused region), and dynamic shapes (symbolic dimensions like batch size or sequence length that prevent static tiling decisions). A beginner thinks fusion is always good — fewer kernel launches, better cache reuse — and assumes the compiler just greedily merges whatever it can. What an expert loses sleep over is that a fusion boundary in the wrong place under dynamic shapes forces you to either emit a family of specialized kernels (combinatorial explosion) or fall back to a conservative generic kernel that destroys the performance you were chasing; the wrong boundary also breaks memory layout contracts between heterogeneous ops, causing silent transposes or padding that cost more than the fusion saved. The deeper trap is that shape-dependent branching in boundary selection must itself be compiled — you're now writing a compiler that emits a runtime dispatcher that selects among compiler outputs, and the correctness and latency of that meta-level logic is where production systems actually fail.

To decide whether to fuse a Tensor Core GEMM with a CUDA-core elementwise epilogue, the compiler needs: the output tile shape of the GEMM (which determines the register file footprint and whether the epilogue fits without spilling), the memory layout of the GEMM output (row-major vs. column-major, and the specific MMA fragment layout which is warp-level and non-trivial — CUTLASS documents these as LayoutC constraints that are instruction-specific), the arithmetic intensity of the epilogue (to judge if it's memory-bound enough to benefit from fusion rather than a separate vectorized kernel), and the occupancy impact of the combined register pressure on the SM. Under dynamic shapes, the tile shape is the critical casualty: CUTLASS and Triton both select tile sizes (e.g., 128×128×32 vs. 64×64×32 threadblock tiles) based on M, N, K dimensions, because the wrong tile on a small matrix causes catastrophic wave quantization — a 128×128 tile on a 130×130 matrix wastes ~97% of the last wave. NVIDIA's CUTLASS 3.x addresses this with the "persistent kernel" and stream-K decomposition, but those require knowing the output shape to partition work; under symbolic shapes, the compiler must either emit a runtime heuristic selector (what TVM's MetaSchedule and XLA's autotuner do, with offline-profiled lookup tables keyed on shape) or conservatively pick a small tile that's safe but slow. The epilogue fusion decision is then doubly dynamic: not only does the tile shape change, but the fragment layout implied by that tile — which determines how epilogue threads map to output elements — changes with it, meaning the epilogue code itself must be regenerated or templated per tile choice, which is exactly why CUTLASS exposes epilogue functors as template parameters rather than runtime callbacks.

The core correctness risk is that tile size selection isn't just a performance knob — it determines the memory access pattern and write-back coverage, and a wrong selection can cause threads to write output elements multiple times (in overlapping tiles), skip elements entirely (coverage gaps at boundary conditions), or use the wrong MMA fragment layout for the epilogue scatter, producing silently wrong numerical output rather than a crash. Concretely, in CUTLASS's warp-specialized kernels (e.g., SM90 Hopper WGMMA), the epilogue assumes a specific TiledMMA configuration that determines which threads own which output registers; if the runtime selector picks a tile configuration whose fragment layout doesn't match the compiled epilogue functor's assumed ownership map, you get threads writing to wrong memory locations — this is undefined behavior that CUDA won't trap, it just produces wrong answers. A subtler risk appears at tensor boundaries: the predication logic that masks out-of-bounds stores is generated assuming a specific tile shape, so a mismatched runtime selection can disable or corrupt those predicates, causing illegal writes into adjacent buffers — a memory safety violation that may only manifest as wrong outputs in a subsequent operator, making it extremely hard to debug. TVM guards against this by treating each (tile_size, epilogue_type) combination as a distinct compiled artifact with its own correctness-verified schedule, then the runtime selector only chooses among pre-validated candidates — the selector itself cannot produce an untested combination. XLA similarly uses "thunk" abstractions where each compiled kernel carries its own shape-constraint predicate that is checked at dispatch time, so an out-of-range shape falls back to a reference implementation rather than executing a mismatched kernel. PyTorch's Inductor takes a weaker approach: it uses guards (shape range assertions compiled into the dispatcher) that trigger recompilation when violated, which is correct but means the first execution of an out-of-guard shape pays full recompilation cost rather than falling back gracefully. The general lesson real systems have learned is that the runtime selector must be closed over the same shape constraints used during code generation — any shape reaching the selector that wasn't in the compiler's assumption set must be explicitly routed to a fallback, and the dangerous gap is that verifying this closure property is undecidable in general for symbolic shape expressions.

When a bias add inside the epilogue has broadcast semantics that depend on runtime shape — batch=1 means broadcast the bias across all rows, batch>1 means elementwise addition with a full bias tensor — the fusion boundary decision forks because the two cases require different memory access patterns in the epilogue: the broadcast case reads one bias value per column and reuses it across the threadblock's row tiles, while the batched case reads a distinct bias row per batch element, changing the pointer arithmetic and predication logic baked into the compiled kernel. This isn't resolvable statically under dynamic shapes because the condition batch == 1 is a runtime predicate, so the compiler must either (a) emit two fully compiled epilogue variants and a runtime branch selecting between them, or (b) emit a single "general" epilogue that always does the batched access pattern but with stride=0 for the broadcast case — option (b) is what CUTLASS's VisitorTree epilogue framework does, encoding broadcast as a strided tensor with zero batch stride, which unifies the code path at the cost of an extra stride multiplication per thread that is otherwise free in the broadcast-specialized path. XLA's broadcast semantic analysis (in hlo_instruction.cc) attempts to canonicalize broadcasts into explicit reshape+tile operations before fusion, which means the shape-dependence is pushed above the fusion pass — but this only works when XLA can prove the broadcast is unconditional, and dynamic batch falls through to a runtime specialization via its "dynamic padder" infrastructure that emits shape checks before kernel dispatch. TVM's Relax IR handles this more explicitly: shape-dependent control flow is represented as R.match_cast and rx.if nodes in the IRModule, so the fusion pass sees a genuine branch in the graph and must decide whether to fuse both branches independently (producing two fused kernels under an if-then-else dispatch) or to unfuse the bias add and leave it as a separate kernel that always runs the general path. The practical industry answer — visible in how torch.compile handles this — is to specialize aggressively: the first time batch=1 is seen, compile a broadcast-specialized fused kernel; the first time batch=8 is seen, compile a batched fused kernel; guards (torch._dynamo shape guards) ensure the right variant runs, and the compilation cache keys on the resolved predicate value. The expert worry here is guard explosion: each shape-dependent predicate in the epilogue multiplies the number of compiled variants, and a model with 10 such predicates in its epilogue tree could in principle require 2^10 compiled kernels, which is why systems like JAX's JIT and TensorRT both implement predicate merging heuristics to find the minimal set of specializations that covers the expected shape distribution without combinatorial blowup.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2681)

The principled strategies cluster into three families: profile-guided specialization (specialize on predicates whose values are empirically stable across runs), cost-model-driven specialization (specialize only when the performance delta between the specialized and general path exceeds a threshold that amortizes recompilation cost), and predicate dependency analysis (identify which predicates are correlated — if batch=1 implies seq_len=1 in a transformer's KV-cache path, they collapse to one specialization axis, not two). TensorRT's polygraphy and engine-building pipeline exemplifies the first: it profiles the shape distribution of a deployment workload and then builds optimization profiles (min/opt/max shape tuples) that cover observed shapes, explicitly refusing to specialize outside those profiles — the operator making the tradeoff is the deployment engineer who supplies the shape ranges, not the compiler. torch.compile's approach is more automatic but cruder: it specializes on the first observed value of each dynamic dimension by default, then widens to a symbolic range if that dimension varies, using a "constraint propagation" pass in torch/_dynamo/variables/ to detect which guards are redundant given others — but it has no explicit cost model for the specialization decision, so it will happily generate dozens of recompilations for a model with genuinely variable shapes until the recompile limit (torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit, default 8) triggers a fallback to fully dynamic (slow) mode. The most principled published approach is the "equality saturation over shape predicates" idea implicit in MLIR's shape inference passes and made explicit in the Nimble system (OSDI 2021), which represents shape functions symbolically and finds equivalence classes of shapes that map to the same optimal kernel — specialization happens at equivalence-class boundaries rather than at individual predicate values, which can reduce the variant count from exponential to linear in the number of independent shape axes. In practice, the decision is almost never made by a single principled agent: TVM AutoScheduler decides tile-level specialization, a separate fusion pass decides operator-boundary specialization, and the runtime dispatcher handles predicate evaluation — these components don't share a global budget, so the system can over-specialize on cheap predicates while under-specializing on expensive ones. The honest state of the art is that no deployed system fully solves this: JAX/XLA's jax.jit with abstracted_axes and torch.compile's dynamic=True both punt the hardest tradeoffs to the user, who must manually annotate which dimensions are dynamic, effectively outsourcing the predicate selection decision to whoever wrote the model training loop.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2682)
response:
When a compiler has collapsed two correlated predicates — say, batch=1 ↔ seq_len=512 observed during training — into a single specialization axis, it has effectively compiled a kernel whose correctness predicate is a conjunction: the kernel is only valid when both conditions hold simultaneously. At inference with variable batch, the conjunction breaks but the system may not know which half broke: the runtime guard checks batch=1 and finds it false, triggering recompilation, but if the new compilation re-runs correlation analysis on the (now absent) training-time shape distribution, it may produce a different collapsed assumption that is equally fragile, rather than treating batch and seq_len as genuinely independent axes. TensorRT handles this via its optimization profile mechanism — if an input shape falls outside all registered profiles, it returns an error rather than silently executing a mismatched kernel, forcing the user to rebuild the engine with updated profiles; this is correct but operationally brutal, as it means a TensorRT deployment that encounters an out-of-profile shape at inference time simply fails rather than degrading gracefully. torch.compile's recovery path is recompilation with widened guards: the GuardManager in Dynamo detects the violated guard, invalidates the compiled artifact, and retraces with the new shape, but it has no mechanism to learn that the original correlation was spurious — it will re-collapse the axes if the new trace happens to observe a shape that re-satisfies the correlation, meaning the fragility is latent and will resurface. The detection problem is genuinely hard because correlation assumptions are implicit in the compiled artifact — they're not stored as first-class metadata in most systems — so recovering them requires either re-running the full shape analysis on the original graph (expensive) or instrumenting the compiler to emit correlation certificates alongside each kernel (what MLIR's shape constraint dialect is moving toward, but not yet production-complete). The most robust production pattern, used in Meta's inference stack for large models, is to not trust training-time shape distributions at all: shapes are treated as fully symbolic at compile time, correlation analysis is disabled, and specialization happens only on predicates that can be proven invariant from the model architecture itself (e.g., head dimension in attention is always 64 for a given model checkpoint) — this sacrifices some peak performance but eliminates the class of silent correlation violations entirely. The deeper lesson is that correlation-based collapsing is a form of inductive bias baked into compiled code, and compiled code has no native mechanism for detecting that its inductive biases have been falsified — the field is missing a standard interface between the runtime shape observation system and the compiler's assumption registry, and every production system has either a bespoke solution or no solution at all.

The minimum certificate is a set of linear arithmetic constraints over the runtime-observable shape integers — specifically, a conjunction of affine equalities and inequalities of the form a₁·d₁ + a₂·d₂ + ... ≤ c where the dᵢ are tensor dimension values readable directly from the input descriptors at dispatch time — because linear arithmetic over integers is decidable in O(n) per constraint evaluation and requires no symbolic reasoning, just integer arithmetic on already-available values. Each constraint must also carry a validity domain: the range of dimension values over which the compiler actually verified the constraint holds (e.g., batch ∈ [1, 512]), because an affine relationship that holds over the training distribution may be a coincidence that breaks outside it, and the runtime needs to know when to distrust the certificate entirely rather than just check the constraint. Beyond the constraints themselves, the certificate needs a kernel variant tag that bijectively identifies which compiled artifact the constraints protect — without this, a runtime that invalidates one certificate doesn't know which cached kernels to evict, and can silently continue using a now-uncertified kernel if the dispatch table isn't keyed correctly. The practical encoding is close to what ONNX Runtime's EP (execution provider) interface does with its GetCapability and shape-validation metadata: each subgraph delegated to an EP carries a shape predicate function pointer and a validity range, evaluated at runtime in a single pass over the input shapes before dispatch — the overhead is typically under 1 microsecond for models with fewer than ~100 shape constraints, which is negligible against kernel launch latency. What the certificate must not contain is anything requiring tensor values rather than tensor shapes — value-dependent branching (e.g., a mask that's all-zeros for some inputs) looks like a shape predicate to the model author but requires reading actual data, blowing up validation cost from O(rank) to O(elements). The open gap is nonlinear shape relationships — attention's seq_len² · head_dim memory footprint, or convolution's output size formula — which appear in real models but fall outside affine certificates; systems like Halide's bounds inference and MLIR's polynomial shape functions handle these with interval arithmetic on polynomial expressions, but no production ML runtime has yet standardized a certificate format that includes polynomial constraints alongside linear ones, leaving nonlinear shape relationships either over-approximated (widening to a linear bound that's too conservative) or uncertified entirely.

The fundamental requirement is that tensor descriptor fields read by the host dispatcher — base pointer, byte strides, and dimension sizes — must be host-visible and finalized before the dispatcher evaluates the certificate, which means any device-side operation that writes those fields (e.g., a prior kernel that produces a dynamic shape output and writes it into a descriptor struct in device memory) must have completed and its results propagated to host memory before the certificate check runs. CUDA's memory model makes this treacherous: device writes to cudaMallocManaged memory or explicit cudaMemcpy of descriptor structs are only guaranteed host-visible after a cudaStreamSynchronize or cudaDeviceSynchronize, and a dispatcher that reads descriptor fields from pinned host memory without ensuring the prior kernel's stream has flushed will see stale values — this is not hypothetical, it's the root cause of a class of bugs in eager-mode PyTorch when dynamic shapes are computed by a prior kernel (e.g., torch.unique's output size) and immediately used to dispatch the next operation. CUDA graphs make this substantially worse: in a captured graph, the host dispatcher runs during capture time to record the kernel launch, but the actual tensor descriptors aren't populated until replay time — any certificate check performed at capture time reads uninitialized or placeholder descriptor values, which is why CUDA graph capture with dynamic shapes requires either conditional nodes (cudaGraphAddConditionalNode, introduced in CUDA 12.3) or external semaphores that break the graph to allow host re-dispatch, both of which carry 5–15 microsecond overhead per break point that erases much of the graph's latency advantage. TensorRT's approach with dynamic shapes sidesteps some of this by requiring that all shape inputs be provided to the runtime as explicit "shape tensors" — small host-side integer arrays separate from the data tensors — whose values are guaranteed CPU-visible before engine execution begins, effectively creating a two-class system where shape information never lives purely on device during dispatch. PyTorch's torch.compile with CUDA graphs uses "dynamic shape cudagraphs" that re-capture whenever a new shape is observed, which avoids the stale-descriptor problem but means the first inference at each new shape pays full capture overhead (~50–200ms for large models), and the capture itself must be preceded by a warm-up run that forces all descriptor values to be CPU-visible. The place current runtimes most reliably get this wrong is with in-graph shape computation: when a shape value is the output of a device kernel (not a user-provided input), most runtimes lack a clean abstraction for "this value is a shape that the dispatcher needs before the next kernel launches," and instead either force an implicit synchronization (correct but slow) or speculatively read the descriptor without synchronizing (fast but silently wrong when the prior kernel hasn't flushed).
